places.note: bridge over the Marne just above its confluence with the Seine
places.summary: The bridge at Charenton crossed the Marne just above its confluence with the Seine, carrying the road south-east out of Paris. The present bridge carries the N6 between Charenton-le-Pont and Alfortville.

places.note: the stone bridge of 1500–1512, lined with houses; rebuilt 1853 and 1919
places.summary: One of the oldest crossing points in Paris. The stone bridge of 1500–1512, lined with houses on both sides, is the one drawn here; it was replaced in 1853 by the present bridge, whose arches were reduced from five to three in 1912.

The 'little bridge' between the Île de la Cité and the Left Bank, on the line of the old Roman road. It was rebuilt many times; the present bridge dates from 1853 and was renamed Petit-Pont–Cardinal-Lustiger in 2013.
Named after the money-changers who kept their shops on it. The bridge on this map, lined with houses, linked the Cité to the Grand Châtelet; the present bridge dates from 1858–1860.
A bridge built over a row of water mills, just downstream of the Pont au Change. It collapsed in 1596; its successor, the Pont Marchand, burned in 1621 and was never rebuilt.
Links the Left Bank (place Saint-Michel) to the Île de la Cité. The bridge on the map was lined with houses; the present bridge was built in 1857.

places.note: Pont d'Arcans; small bridge on a stream west of the city; unresolved

places.modern: Place des Vosges (built on part of its site)
places.summary: A cluster of royal buildings that grew from the 14th century north of today's place des Vosges. Louis XII and Henri II both died here. After Henri II's death in 1559 Catherine de' Medici abandoned it; it was sold off and demolished, and the place Royale (place des Vosges) was laid out on part of its grounds.

places.note: Hôtel d'Angoulême near the Tournelles; unresolved
Hôtel du Prévôt de Paris (Hugues Aubriot's house near Saint-Paul)
places.summary: An old town house in the Saint-Paul quarter, at what is now 16 rue Charlemagne. It was demolished in 1891.

places.note: the queen's lodgings of the Hôtel Saint-Pol, the royal residence of Charles V
places.summary: The queen's lodgings in the Hôtel Saint-Pol, the rambling royal residence that Charles V assembled from four properties in 1361–1365. The estate was broken up and built over from 1544, which created the rue Neuve-Saint-Paul (rue Charles-V), the rue des Lions-Saint-Paul and the rue de la Cerisaie.

places.note: the college of Tournai, founded in 1353 next to the college of Boncourt; the label calls it 'l'ostel'
places.summary: A college of the University of Paris founded in 1353 by Gilles de Lorris, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, at the same time as the neighbouring college of Boncourt. It was later united with the college of Navarre.

places.note: the Renaissance building begun in 1533 was burned in 1871 and rebuilt
places.summary: The seat of the Paris city government since 1357, on the place de Grève. The Renaissance building begun in 1533 was still unfinished when this map was made. It was burned during the Commune in 1871 and rebuilt in the same style.

places.note: fortified gate at the left-bank end of the Petit-Pont; demolished 1782
places.summary: A small fortress guarding the Left Bank end of the Petit-Pont, the counterpart of the Grand Châtelet on the Right Bank. It served as a prison and was demolished in 1782.

places.note: fortress guarding the Pont au Change; seat of the Prévôté; demolished 1802–1810
places.summary: The fortress at the Right Bank end of the Pont au Change, built by Louis VI where the rue Saint-Denis met the river. It housed the court and prison of the Prévôté of Paris. It was demolished in 1802–1810; the place du Châtelet now occupies its site.
The clock tower at the north-east corner of the royal palace, now part of the Palais de Justice and the Conciergerie. Its clock was the first public clock in Paris.

The part of the royal palace of the Cité that became a prison in 1370, when the kings stopped living there. Two great medieval halls survive. During the Revolution, Marie-Antoinette and some 2,780 other prisoners were held and tried here.

places.note: royal palace, later the seat of the Parlement; partly survives inside the Palais de Justice
places.summary: The palace of the kings of France from the 10th to the 14th century, at the west end of the Île de la Cité. After the kings left, it remained the seat of the highest courts, as it still is: the Palais de Justice stands on the site and incorporates the Conciergerie and the Sainte-Chapelle.

places.note: its building in the palace burned in 1737
places.summary: The royal court of accounts, which audited the Crown's finances, the ancestor of today's Cour des comptes. Its building stood in the palace precinct and burned in 1737.

places.note: town house of the abbots of Cluny, built c. 1485–1510
places.summary: The town house of the abbots of Cluny, rebuilt in 1485–1510 next to the ruins of the Roman baths. It is one of the few medieval town houses left in Paris and now houses the Musée de Cluny, the national museum of the Middle Ages.

places.note: the old royal mint by the rue de la Monnaie; the mint moved to the quai de Conti in 1775
places.summary: The royal mint stood here, near the rue de la Monnaie that is named after it. In 1775 the mint moved to its present building on the quai de Conti, on the Left Bank.

places.note: the bishop's court and prison; demolished 1783
places.summary: The prison of the bishops of Paris from 1222, later a royal prison, at what is now 19 rue Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois. It was demolished in 1783.

places.note: Hôtel de Nevers; not the later hôtel of 1580 on the Monnaie site; unresolved
Hôtel d'Alençon near the Louvre; unresolved
residence of the dukes of Bourbon by the Louvre; demolished 1660 for the Louvre colonnade
places.summary: The town house of the dukes of Bourbon, facing the east gate of the medieval Louvre. The king confiscated it around 1523 and most of it was destroyed in 1525; its chapel and great hall, later used as a theatre by Molière, survived until 1660, when they made way for the Louvre colonnade.

places.note: the town house / college of the abbots of Saint-Denis, which gave the rue des Grands-Augustins its 13th-century name (Paris street register)
places.summary: Probably the town house and college of the abbots of Saint-Denis, which gave the rue des Grands-Augustins its 13th-century name (rue de l'Abbé-de-Saint-Denis). It has disappeared.

places.note: the name 'Rohan' is a corruption of 'Rouen' (the archbishops of Rouen had their town house here)
places.summary: The archbishops of Rouen had their Paris house here; 'Rohan' is a corruption of 'Rouen'. The courtyards of the Cour de Rohan, off the cour du Commerce-Saint-André, still survive.

places.note: in 1550 the medieval castle was being rebuilt: Lescot's wing was begun in 1546
places.summary: In 1550 the medieval castle of the Louvre was being transformed: Pierre Lescot's Renaissance wing was begun in 1546 for François I. The palace grew for three more centuries and became a museum in 1793.

places.note: the Wikipedia article covers the Tour de Nesle, the corner tower of the hôtel
places.modern: Institut de France and Monnaie de Paris (on its site)
places.summary: A great town house on the Left Bank, built against Philip Augustus's city wall, whose corner tower was the Tour de Nesle. The Institut de France and the Monnaie de Paris stand on its site.
A Cistercian abbey east of the city, around which the faubourg Saint-Antoine grew up. The Hôpital Saint-Antoine (12th arrondissement) now occupies its buildings.

A monastery of the Celestine order founded in the 14th century near the Bastille. After Saint-Denis it was the most important royal burial place in France: many princes were buried in its church. It has completely disappeared.

An old collegiate church at the southern exit of Paris, on the boundary of today's 5th and 13th arrondissements. It appears on many historic plans of Paris, including this one. Most of it was destroyed in the early 19th century; the last remains disappeared in 1874.

places.note: church of Saint-Hippolyte in the faubourg Saint-Marcel; demolished 1807
places.summary: The parish church of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, in what is now the Croulebarbe quarter of the 13th arrondissement. It has disappeared.

places.note: a hospital in the faubourg Saint-Marcel; unresolved

places.summary: A convent of Poor Clares founded in 1289 in the faubourg Saint-Marcel at the request of Queen Marguerite de Provence. The rue de Julienne, the rue Pascal and the rue des Cordelières were laid out across its grounds.

places.old: S. CATERINE DU VAL DES ESCOLIERS
places.note: printed S. CATERINNE DU VAL DES ECOLIERS
places.summary: A priory founded by the sergeants-at-arms of the royal guard to commemorate the victory of Bouvines (1214). It was demolished at the end of the 18th century; the place du Marché-Sainte-Catherine was laid out on its site.

places.note: parish of the royal Hôtel Saint-Pol; demolished 1796–1799
places.summary: The parish church of the royal Hôtel Saint-Pol, on the rue Saint-Paul at the corner of today's rue Neuve-Saint-Pierre. It became a parish in 1125 and the royal parish in the 14th century; it was demolished in 1796–1799.
A convent on the rue de l'Ave-Maria in the Saint-Gervais quarter. It has disappeared; the street keeps its name.
The parish church of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, at 141 rue Mouffetard, built between the 15th and 18th centuries. It still serves as a parish church.

places.note: the church of the Templars' (later Hospitallers') enclosure
places.summary: The headquarters of the Knights Templar in France, later the main house of the Hospitallers of Saint John. Until the Revolution the Temple enclosure kept its own jurisdiction inside Paris; Louis XVI was imprisoned in its keep. The square du Temple occupies part of its site.

places.note: orphanage founded 1534; the Marché des Enfants-Rouges keeps its name
places.summary: Founded in the 1530s as the first Paris institution devoted solely to foundlings; the children were dressed in red. It became a barracks in 1808. The quarter and the Marché des Enfants-Rouges keep its name.

places.note: chapel of Braque (Notre-Dame de Braque); unresolved
the Petit Saint-Antoine (Hospitallers of Saint-Anthony), rue Saint-Antoine
places.summary: The Petit Saint-Antoine, a house of the Hospitallers of Saint Anthony on the rue Saint-Antoine, who cared for sufferers of 'Saint Anthony's fire' (ergotism). It has disappeared.

An abbey of canons regular founded in the 12th century by William of Champeaux. Within a few decades it became one of the great centres of theology and philosophy in medieval Europe. It was demolished after the Revolution; the Jussieu university campus stands on its site.

places.note: the cloister of c. 1427 survives; the church was rebuilt in 1756
places.summary: The church of the Billettes friars, at 24 rue des Archives. The present church was built in 1754–1758, but its cloister of the early 15th century survives: it is the only medieval cloister left in Paris. Today it is a Lutheran church.
The cemetery of the parish church of Saint-Jean-en-Grève, behind the Hôtel de Ville. It disappeared with the church, which was demolished in 1797–1800.

The church on the place Saint-Gervais, east of the Hôtel de Ville. The present Gothic church was built from 1494 and its classical façade added in 1616–1621, so in 1550 it was a building site. It is still a parish church.
A parish church near the Hôtel de Ville, first the baptismal chapel of nearby Saint-Gervais. It became a parish in 1212, was rebuilt in 1326 and was demolished in 1797–1800.
The cemetery of the parish of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs, on the rue Beaubourg. It has disappeared; the rue du Cimetière-Saint-Nicolas (now part of rue Chapon) was named after it.

places.note: cloister of the canons of Saint-Merri
places.summary: The enclosure of the canons of Saint-Merri around their church. The rue du Cloître-Saint-Merri keeps its name.

The church of Saint-Merri on the rue Saint-Martin, by the Centre Pompidou, named after the abbot Médéric. The present Flamboyant Gothic church was built in 1500–1550, so it was brand new when this map was made.

places.note: hospital of the Saint-Esprit-en-Grève, beside the Hôtel de Ville
places.summary: A charitable institution beside the Hôtel de Ville that took in poor and abandoned children. It has disappeared.

places.note: the canons' quarter north of the cathedral
places.summary: The canons' quarter of Notre-Dame, occupying the north-east quarter of the Île de la Cité between today's rue d'Arcole and the quai aux Fleurs. A few of its old houses survive in the rue Chanoinesse.

A small church just behind the apse of Notre-Dame, on the site of today's square Jean-XXIII. It was the fifth station on the pilgrimage route from Paris to the basilica of Saint-Denis. It was demolished in the early 19th century.
A Cistercian college of the old University of Paris, built from 1248. Until the Revolution it housed monks studying in Paris. Its great Gothic hall survives and is used today as a cultural centre.

The church on the corner of the rue des Bernardins and the rue Saint-Victor. The present church was built from the second half of the 17th century on the site of a 13th-century church, and only finished in 1937.

The parish church of the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, next to the Panthéon. It replaced a 13th-century church and was built from the end of the 15th century to 1624, so the map shows it under construction.

places.modern: Lycée Henri-IV (on its site; the Tour Clovis survives)
places.summary: An Augustinian abbey on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, founded on the tomb of the patron saint of Paris. Several of its buildings, including the Tour Clovis, survive as the Lycée Henri-IV; the Panthéon was built as its new church.

The church of the faubourg Saint-Laurent, on the old Roman road north from Paris (today's rue du Faubourg-Saint-Martin). It still stands, at the junction of the boulevards de Strasbourg and de Magenta.
The church of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs on the rue Saint-Martin, built in five stages between 1420 and 1620, mostly in Flamboyant Gothic. It is still a parish church.

A priory founded in 1059 and given to the monks of Cluny in 1079; it became the most important Cluniac house after Cluny itself. Its church and refectory survive as part of the Musée des Arts et Métiers.

places.note: chapel and hospital of the minstrels' guild
places.summary: The chapel and hospital of the guild of minstrels and musicians, on the rue Saint-Martin. It has disappeared.
A large parish church founded in the 12th century and enlarged in the 14th and 16th centuries. It was demolished at the end of the 18th century; only its bell tower survives, the Tour Saint-Jacques.
A parish church on the Île de la Cité, near the river. It has disappeared.

places.note: church of Saint-Martial in the Cité; label reading uncertain
places.summary: A church on the Île de la Cité, behind Saint-Éloi, near the Palais de Justice. It has disappeared.
A parish church on the Île de la Cité. It has disappeared.

places.note: church of Saint-Christophe, in front of Notre-Dame; demolished 1747
places.summary: A small church in front of Notre-Dame, one of the oldest in the Cité, linked to the Hôtel-Dieu. It was demolished in 1747 to enlarge the parvis.
A small church on the Île de la Cité dedicated to Saint Genevieve, on what is now the parvis of Notre-Dame. It has disappeared.
A parish church on the Île de la Cité. It has disappeared.
The cathedral of Paris, begun in 1163 under bishop Maurice de Sully. It was already almost 400 years old when this map was made. It survived the fire of April 2019 and reopened in December 2024.

places.note: in 1550 it stood on the south side of the parvis, straddling the small arm of the Seine
places.summary: The oldest hospital in Paris, traditionally founded by bishop Saint Landry around 650. In 1550 it stood on the south side of the parvis, with buildings reaching across the small arm of the Seine. It was rebuilt on the north side of the parvis in 1867–1878.

A small medieval church on the Left Bank, in the square René-Viviani facing Notre-Dame. One of the oldest churches in Paris, it has been used by the Melkite Greek Catholic Church since the end of the 19th century.
A chapel on the rue Saint-Jacques dedicated to Saint Yves, patron saint of lawyers, founded in the 14th century by Breton students. It has disappeared.

places.note: convent of the Carmelites (Grands-Carmes) on the place Maubert
places.summary: The Great Carmelite convent next to the place Maubert, at the foot of the rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève. It has disappeared; the 5th arrondissement police station stands on its site.
A house of the Knights Hospitaller of Saint John on the Left Bank, where the rue de Latran is today. Its buildings were demolished in the mid-19th century.
A church on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, in use from the 12th century until the Revolution. A few traces survive.
A church at the corner of the rue Saint-Jacques and the old rue Saint-Étienne-des-Grès (now rue Cujas). It has disappeared.
The church on the rue Saint-Jacques at the corner of the rue de l'Abbé-de-l'Épée. The present church was built in 1630–1685, replacing the older chapel of the hospital shown on this map.

places.note: the hospital of the Hospitallers of Altopascio, next to Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas
places.summary: The hospice of the Hospitallers of Altopascio (Haut-Pas) in Tuscany, who looked after pilgrims on the road to Santiago. Its chapel gave its name to the church of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas.

places.note: priory of Notre-Dame-des-Champs; from 1603 the first Carmelite convent in Paris
places.summary: In 1550 a priory of Notre-Dame-des-Champs stood here, south of the city. In 1603 it became the first convent of the Discalced Carmelites in Paris, which attracted nuns from the high nobility. It was closed at the Revolution and demolished in 1797.

The leper house of Saint-Lazare, in a large enclosure north of the city, in today's 10th arrondissement. From 1632 it was the headquarters of Vincent de Paul's congregation, and after the Revolution a prison.

places.note: cemetery of the hospital of the Trinité
places.summary: The cemetery of the hospital of the Trinité, on the rue Saint-Denis. It has disappeared.
A hostel for pilgrims on the way to Santiago de Compostela, in the block between the rues Saint-Denis, Mauconseil, Mondétour and du Cygne. It was demolished in 1823.
A 13th-century church at 92 rue Saint-Denis. It is still a parish church.
A Benedictine abbey on the rue Saint-Denis. The monks moved out in 1572 and it has disappeared.

places.note: church and hospital of the Saint-Sépulcre, rue Saint-Denis
places.summary: A church and hospice of the Holy Sepulchre on the rue Saint-Denis. It has disappeared.

places.note: church and cemetery of the Saints-Innocents; the cemetery was emptied into the Catacombs in 1786–1788
places.modern: Place Joachim-du-Bellay (the Fontaine des Innocents survives)
places.summary: The largest cemetery in Paris, by the Halles, named after the church of the Holy Innocents at its corner. It was closed in 1780 and the remains were moved to the Catacombs. The place Joachim-du-Bellay now covers it; the Renaissance Fontaine des Innocents, carved in 1549, stands in the middle.
A church near the Halles. It has disappeared; the place Sainte-Opportune keeps its name.
A hospital at the corner of the rue Saint-Denis and the rue des Lombards, where nuns sheltered poor women and buried the unclaimed dead. It was demolished in 1853.
A small church beside the Grand Châtelet. It was demolished in 1684 when the Châtelet was enlarged.
A parish church on the Île de la Cité, rebuilt in the 15th century and demolished at the end of the 18th century.

places.note: church of Saint-Barthélemy in the Cité, the palace parish
places.summary: The parish church of the royal palace on the Île de la Cité, facing the palace across the rue de la Barillerie. It has disappeared.
A convent church on the Île de la Cité, later the church of the Barnabites, on the site now occupied by the Préfecture de police (2 rue de Lutèce).

places.note: handwritten addition on the Basel copy
places.summary: The palace chapel built for Saint Louis to house the Crown of Thorns and other relics of the Passion that he acquired from 1239; it was consecrated in 1248. Its upper chapel is famous for its stained glass. The label was added by hand on the Basel copy of this map.

places.note: chapel of Saint-Michel in the palace courtyard
places.summary: A chapel in the courtyard of the royal palace on the Île de la Cité. It has disappeared.
A Flamboyant Gothic church in the Latin Quarter, near the Seine, with the only surviving medieval charnel-house cloister in Paris. It is still a parish church.

The Paris house of the Trinitarian friars, known as Mathurins, from the early 13th century until 1790. It occupied the block now bounded by the rue Saint-Jacques, the boulevard Saint-Germain, the Hôtel de Cluny and the rue Du Sommerard.
An ancient church on the rue Saint-Jacques, founded in the 6th century. It was demolished in 1831 for the Théâtre du Panthéon, which in turn made way for the rue des Écoles in 1854.

A church built in 1427 at the corner of the rue de la Harpe and the rue des Cordeliers (now rue de l'École-de-Médecine). It was the religious centre of the surgeons who founded the Academy of Surgery. It was demolished around 1836.

places.note: the Dominican convent of the rue Saint-Jacques (Jacobins)
places.summary: The great Dominican convent of the rue Saint-Jacques, founded in the early 13th century. It gave the Dominicans their French name, Jacobins, after the street. Thomas Aquinas taught here. It has disappeared.

A convent of nuns who first served the hospital of Saint-Gervais and took in reformed prostitutes; their house on the rue Saint-Denis, just inside the Porte Saint-Denis, appears here. It has disappeared; the rue d'Alexandrie was the rue des Filles-Dieu.
A parish church on the rue Saint-Denis. It has disappeared; the rue Saint-Sauveur keeps its name.

The chapel of the goldsmiths' guild, dedicated to Saint Eligius, founded in the early 15th century and rebuilt in the mid-16th century — just when this map was made. It was destroyed at the end of the 18th century; traces of its façade survive at 8 rue des Orfèvres.
A parish church on the place Saint-André-des-Arts, demolished in the early 19th century. The square was laid out on its site.

places.modern: Couvent des Cordeliers (only the refectory survives)
places.summary: The great Franciscan convent founded with the support of Saint Louis, in the Latin Quarter. During the Revolution it was the seat of the Cordeliers club. Only its refectory survives, at 15 rue de l'École-de-Médecine.

places.modern: Jardin du Luxembourg (part of its site)
places.summary: A Carthusian monastery founded in 1257 at Vauvert with the support of Saint Louis, south of the city. It was demolished in 1796–1800; part of its grounds is now in the Jardin du Luxembourg.

places.note: the present church was begun in 1532 and finished in 1637; the map still shows the older church
places.summary: The parish church of the Halles. The present church, the third largest in Paris, was begun in 1532 and completed in 1637; this map still shows the older church it replaced.
A convent of reformed women, the Filles Pénitentes, founded at the end of the 15th century. In 1572 they moved to the former abbey of Saint-Magloire on the rue Saint-Denis.
The parish church of the Louvre, facing the palace's east front. It has been called the 'parish of the artists'. Its bell gave the signal for the Saint Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572.
A large Augustinian friary on the Left Bank by the Seine, whose name survives in the quai and rue des Grands-Augustins. It was destroyed during the Revolution.

places.note: chapel of the Martyrs on the slope of Montmartre
places.modern: Chapelle du Martyre, rue Yvonne-Le-Tac (near the site)
places.summary: A chapel on the slope of Montmartre, on the spot where Saint Denis was believed to have been martyred. It belonged to the abbey of Montmartre. A modern chapel of the Martyrdom stands near the site, on the rue Yvonne-Le-Tac.
A collegiate church on the rue Saint-Honoré, in today's 1st arrondissement. It has disappeared; buildings of the Ministry of Culture stand on its site.
The church of the faubourg Saint-Germain. The present church, the second largest in Paris, was begun in 1646 to replace the church shown here.

places.note: the hospital for the blind founded by Saint Louis; it moved to the faubourg Saint-Antoine in 1780
places.summary: The hospital for 300 (fifteen score: quinze-vingts) blind people founded by Saint Louis, on the rue Saint-Honoré near the Louvre. In 1780 it moved to the faubourg Saint-Antoine (28 rue de Charenton), where it is still the national eye hospital.
A collegiate church near the Louvre. It was demolished in 1739 and replaced by the church of Saint-Louis-du-Louvre, which has also disappeared.

places.note: the abbey church survives; the abbey buildings are gone
places.summary: A Benedictine abbey founded in the mid-6th century by the Merovingian king Childebert I and Saint Germain, bishop of Paris. The abbey church survives as the oldest church in Paris; the monastery buildings have gone.

places.note: the Minims of Chaillot, called the Bonshommes
places.summary: A convent of Minim friars, known as the Bonshommes, in the village of Nigeon (Chaillot), west of Paris. It has disappeared.
A college of the University of Paris founded by Cardinal Jean Lemoine (d. 1313). The rue du Cardinal-Lemoine keeps its name.
A college founded in 1353 on the rue Bordelle (now rue Descartes) by Pierre Becoud, whose name was corrupted into 'Boncourt'. It was later united with the college of Navarre.
A college of the University of Paris on the rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève, also called the college de la Marche-Winville. It has disappeared.

A college founded in 1304 by Queen Joan I of Navarre, wife of Philip IV, on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève. It was one of the most prestigious colleges of the university. Its site was later taken over by the École polytechnique.
A college of the University of Paris near the Porte Saint-Victor. It has disappeared.
A college for students from the diocese of Cornouaille in Brittany. Its bursars were first housed at the college du Plessis; in 1374 a house was bought for them on the rue du Plâtre (now rue Domat).
A college of the University of Paris near the place Maubert. The philosopher Petrus Ramus was its principal in the 1540s–1560s.

A college founded in 1370 by Cardinal Jean de Dormans, bishop of Beauvais, on the rue du Clos-Bruneau (now rue Jean-de-Beauvais). Its Gothic chapel survives as the Romanian Orthodox church of Saint-Jean-de-Beauvais.

places.note: the Écoles de Décret, the law faculty
places.summary: The 'Schools of Decretals', home of the faculty of canon law of the old University of Paris, on the rue Jean-de-Beauvais. The faculty was closed in 1793 and refounded in 1802 as the Paris law school.
A college founded in 1334 for poor students from Lombardy and the rest of Italy. It flourished until the 16th century and was later taken over by Irish priests (the college des Irlandais).

A small college on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, founded in the mid-15th century by Nicolas Coqueret. Around 1547 the humanist Jean Dorat became its principal and taught Ronsard and Du Bellay here, the poets of the Pléiade.
A college on the rue Saint-Jacques next to the college of Clermont (Louis-le-Grand). Its buildings were demolished in 1864 for the northern part of the present Lycée Louis-le-Grand.
A college of the University of Paris from 1412 to 1762, founded by Guy de Roye, archbishop of Reims.
A college founded by Cardinal Philippe de Luxembourg, bishop of Le Mans, for ten students from his diocese.
A college of the University of Paris, belonging to the abbey of Marmoutier near Tours, on the rue Saint-Jacques next to the college du Plessis.

Founded in 1460 on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève; until it closed in 1999 it was the oldest school in Paris. Its rebuilt buildings now house the Bibliothèque Sainte-Barbe. Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier studied here.
A college of the University of Paris at what is now 4 rue Cujas. It has disappeared.

places.note: the college Saint-Michel, also called Chanac
places.summary: A college of the University of Paris, also known as the college Saint-Michel. It has disappeared.
A college of the faculty of arts, known for its harsh discipline; Erasmus and Calvin studied here. The Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève was built on its site in 1844–1850.
A college of the University of Paris, also called the college de Torcy. It has disappeared.
A college of the University of Paris, founded in the 14th century by Gervais Chrétien, physician to Charles V. It has disappeared.
A college founded in 1280 on the rue de la Harpe and closed in 1793. The Lycée Saint-Louis stands on its site.
A college of the University of Paris, on the rue de la Harpe. It has disappeared.
A college founded in 1317 on the rue de la Harpe by Bernard de Farges, archbishop of Narbonne, for nine students from his diocese. The future Pope Clement VI studied here.

The college founded in 1257 by Robert de Sorbon with the support of Saint Louis, for students of theology. Its name came to stand for the whole faculty of theology. The present Sorbonne was rebuilt by Richelieu in the 17th century and again in 1885–1901.

A college founded in 1271 by Robert de Sorbon for poor students of the humanities and philosophy, nicknamed the 'little Sorbonne'. It was demolished in the 17th century to make room for the Sorbonne church.

A college of the University of Paris founded in the 13th century for monks of the order of Cluny. Its buildings were seized during the Revolution and disappeared in the 19th century, roughly between the place de la Sorbonne and the rue Cujas.
A medieval college of the University of Paris, later the college de Grandmont. The rue Mignon, laid out on its site, keeps its name.
A college of the University of Paris founded in 1331 by Queen Joan of Burgundy, on the rue des Cordeliers. The École de Médecine was built on its site.

places.note: college of the Bons-Enfants, rue Saint-Honoré
places.summary: A small college of the University of Paris on the rue Saint-Honoré, near the Louvre. The rue des Bons-Enfants keeps its name.

places.note: a bastion of the city wall
places.summary: A bastion of the city wall of Charles V (built 1356–1383). Its eastern part was strengthened with bastions in the mid-16th century, around the time of this map; the wall was demolished in the 17th century and the Grands Boulevards follow its line.
The eastern gate of Paris, on the rue Saint-Antoine next to the Bastille, in the wall of Charles V. It stood from the mid-14th century until the late 18th century.

A fortress built in the 14th century to guard the Porte Saint-Antoine, later a state prison and a symbol of royal despotism. It was stormed on 14 July 1789 and completely demolished; the place de la Bastille covers its site.

places.note: gate in the faubourg Saint-Marcel; label reading uncertain

places.summary: The gate of the rue du Temple in the wall of Charles V (there was also an older gate of the same name in Philip Augustus's wall). It has disappeared; it stood near today's place de la République.

places.note: gate of Philip Augustus's wall, rue Descartes
places.summary: A gate of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, also called the Porte Saint-Marcel or Porte Bordet, on today's rue Descartes. It was built in the early 13th century and demolished in the 17th.

places.note: the medieval gate, not the triumphal arch of 1674
places.modern: Porte Saint-Martin (the triumphal arch of 1674 stands near the site)
places.summary: The gate of the rue Saint-Martin in the wall of Charles V. In 1674 Louis XIV replaced it with the triumphal arch of the Porte Saint-Martin, which stands near the site.
The southern gate of Philip Augustus's wall, on the rue Saint-Jacques, also called the Porte Notre-Dame-des-Champs. It led to the road to Orléans and Santiago de Compostela.

places.note: the medieval gate, not the triumphal arch of 1672
places.modern: Porte Saint-Denis (the triumphal arch of 1672 stands near the site)
places.summary: The gate of the rue Saint-Denis in the wall of Charles V, the ceremonial entrance of kings into Paris. In 1672–1673 Louis XIV replaced it with the triumphal arch of the Porte Saint-Denis.
A gate of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, also called the Porte d'Enfer or Porte Gibard. It was built in the early 13th century and demolished in the 17th.
A gate of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, near today's carrefour de l'Odéon. It was built in the 13th century and demolished in the 17th.
A gate of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, first called the Porte des Cordeliers, near today's carrefour de l'Odéon. It was built in the 13th century and demolished in the 17th.
The gate of the rue Montmartre in the wall of Charles V. There were three successive Porte Montmartre gates along the rue Montmartre as the city walls expanded; all have disappeared.

A corner tower of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, facing the Louvre across the Seine, built in the early 13th century. It is famous from the scandal of the Tour de Nesle (1314) and later legends. The east pavilion of the Institut de France stands on its site.

The western gate of Paris in the wall of Charles V, on the rue Saint-Honoré, leading towards Saint-Germain-en-Laye. There were three successive Porte Saint-Honoré gates as the walls expanded; all have disappeared.

places.note: the Tour du Bois, the riverside end of Charles V's wall by the Louvre

places.summary: A royal forest east of Paris, with the castle of Vincennes. With 995 hectares it is now the largest green space of Paris, in the 12th arrondissement.
France's longest river, the main tributary of the Seine. It joins the Seine between Charenton-le-Pont and Alfortville, at the top of this map.
The river of Paris. On this map it flows from the top (east) to the bottom (west).
A wayside cross on the road east from Paris, near Charonne. The rue de la Croix-Faubin (11th arrondissement) keeps its name.

places.modern: Boulevard Morland (the island was joined to the bank in 1843)
places.summary: An island in the Seine opposite the Arsenal, used for storing timber and hay. In 1843 the arm of the river separating it from the Right Bank was filled in; the boulevard Morland runs along its former channel.
The suburb that grew up outside the Porte Saint-Victor, around the abbey of Saint-Victor.

places.note: the Champ d'Albiac: in the 1540s parts of the clos du Chardonnet were granted to René d'Ablon and d'Albiac for building
places.summary: The 'Champ d'Albiac', open ground of the clos du Chardonnet. At the end of François I's reign (the 1540s) the clos was divided up for building and plots were granted to René d'Ablon and d'Albiac; this map shows it still largely open.
The great royal gallows of Paris, on the hill of Montfaucon near today's place du Colonel-Fabien. It was in use from at least the 11th century to the reign of Louis XIII. Nothing of it remains.
A gate of the earliest medieval wall of the Right Bank, east of Saint-Gervais. Its name survives in the place Baudoyer.

places.note: 'le Terrain', the open ground at the east tip of the Cité
places.summary: Open ground at the eastern tip of the Île de la Cité, behind Notre-Dame, where the cathedral's builders stored stone. The square Jean-XXIII now occupies it.

places.note: the Tournelle, the riverside tower of Philip Augustus's wall on the left bank
places.summary: A fortified tower at the riverside end of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, on the quai that keeps its name, roughly where the restaurant La Tour d'Argent stands. It was later used as a prison for galley convicts.

places.note: the Champ-Gaillard, the ground around the rue Clopin (named after the great house Clopin), next to the college of Navarre
places.summary: The Champ-Gaillard, ground on the slope of the montagne Sainte-Geneviève next to the college of Navarre, crossed by the rue Clopin, which was named after the great house Clopin. It disappeared under the École polytechnique and later buildings.

places.note: the Gobelin family's dye works and mills on the Bièvre
places.summary: The Gobelin family of dyers had their works and mills on the Bièvre here from the 15th century. In 1601 Henri IV installed a tapestry workshop in their buildings, which became the royal Manufacture des Gobelins in 1662; it is still active at 42 avenue des Gobelins.
The suburb outside the Porte Saint-Jacques, along the road to Orléans, with the hospice of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas and several convents.

places.note: a real-tennis court near the Halles
the mill of the Mint, on the Seine
the palace garden at the west tip of the Cité
places.modern: Place Dauphine and square du Vert-Galant (on its site)
places.summary: The garden of the royal palace at the western tip of the Île de la Cité. After the Pont Neuf was built (1578–1607) the place Dauphine was laid out on this ground.

places.old: LE PRES OU ER DE LOTEL DIEU
places.note: meadow of the Hôtel-Dieu; reading uncertain
in 1550 still the tile kilns that gave the Tuileries their name; the palace was begun in 1564
places.summary: In 1550 this was still an area of tile kilns (tuileries) outside the city wall. Catherine de' Medici began a palace here in 1564, with a garden; the palace burned in 1871, but the Jardin des Tuileries remains.

places.note: the students' meadow of the University
places.summary: The 'clerks' meadow', the riverside meadow of the University's students west of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, notorious for brawls and duels. The rue du Pré-aux-Clercs (7th arrondissement) keeps its name.

places.note: the hay port (Port au Foin) on the Grève
places.summary: The hay port on the Seine below the place de Grève, where boats unloaded hay for the city's horses.
The square in front of the Hôtel de Ville, called the place de Grève until 1803. It sloped down to a sandy river bank (grève) where boats unloaded; it was also the place of public executions.
The calf market, near the Grande Boucherie and the Grand Châtelet. The rue de la Vieille-Place-aux-Veaux, which kept its memory, disappeared in the 19th century.
A square at the foot of the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, one of the oldest market places of the Left Bank. The printer and humanist Étienne Dolet was burned here in 1546.

places.note: the Grande Boucherie, the main butchers' market, by the Grand Châtelet
places.summary: The Grande Boucherie, the main butchers' market of Paris, next to the Grand Châtelet; its guild built the church of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie. It disappeared in the 19th century; the Tour Saint-Jacques stands nearby.
The pillory of the Halles, an octagonal tower with a turning wooden wheel in which offenders were exhibited to the crowd. It was demolished in the 18th century.

places.note: the grain hall in the Halles
places.summary: The grain hall of the medieval Halles. The later Halle au blé of the 18th century, now the Bourse de commerce, stands a short distance west.
The butchers' market of Beauvais at the Halles. It has disappeared.

places.note: the Croix du Trahoir, a cross and place of execution at the corner of rue de l'Arbre-Sec
places.modern: Fontaine de la Croix-du-Trahoir (rebuilt 1776, on the site)
places.summary: A cross at the corner of the rue Saint-Honoré and the rue de l'Arbre-Sec, also a place of execution. A public fountain stood here from the 16th century; it was rebuilt in 1776 and still stands.
A great annual fair held in the faubourg Saint-Germain from 1486 until the Revolution, first held in the 12th century. The Marché Saint-Germain stands on its site.
The pillory of the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which had its own justice over the faubourg. It has disappeared.
The pig market. It moved several times over the centuries; on this map it is in the faubourg Saint-Honoré, west of the city.

places.note: the Grande rue Saint-Antoine; its western end is now rue François-Miron
places.summary: The great road east to the Porte Saint-Antoine and the Bastille, on the line of an old Roman road. It once ran from the rue des Barres to the place de la Bastille; the western stretch was renamed rue François-Miron in 1865.

places.note: called rue des Célestins on some 16th-century plans
places.summary: An old street by the Célestins convent, recorded in 1358 with the crude name 'Pute-y-Muse', which was softened over time into 'Petit-Musc'. Some 16th-century plans, like this one, call it the rue des Célestins.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: A street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, called the rue de la Barre in 1540. It was renamed after Scipion Sardini, an Italian banker who built a house here in the 1560s.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: A street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel built in the 12th century. Its two parts, the rue de la Muette and the rue Permoulin, were later joined under the name rue du Fer-à-Moulin.

places.note: one of several 'rue Neuve' near Saint-Marcel; unresolved

places.summary: A street of dyers in the faubourg Saint-Marcel, by the Bièvre whose water they used. It is now part of the rue Saint-Hippolyte.

places.note: old rue des Cordelières, now rues Broca, Edouard-Quénu and Léon-Maurice-Nordmann
places.summary: Named after the Cordelières convent, this was part of the old rue de Lourcine in the faubourg Saint-Marcel, created in the 12th century. It was split and renamed in the 20th century: rue Edouard-Quénu (1938), rue Broca and rue Léon-Maurice-Nordmann.

places.summary: In the Marais, once called the rue Tougin and later part of the rue de Thorigny, now the rue de la Perle.

places.note: rue de la Culture-Sainte-Catherine, renamed rue de Sévigné in 1867
places.summary: The rue de la Culture-Sainte-Catherine, which ran past the fields (culture) of the priory of Sainte-Catherine. It was renamed rue de Sévigné in 1867 after the letter-writer Madame de Sévigné, who lived at the Hôtel Carnavalet on this street.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: The rue Percée ('pierced' street, cut through a block), called rue Percié by Guillot in 1300. It was renamed rue du Prévôt in 1877.

places.summary: The street of the church of Saint-Paul, already in existence in the mid-14th century. It still runs from the quai to the rue Saint-Antoine.

places.summary: A street along the inside of Philip Augustus's wall in the Saint-Paul quarter, earlier simply the rue des Jardins. A long stretch of the wall still stands along it.

places.summary: Laid out from 1544 on the site of the Hôtel de Saint-Maur, part of the royal Hôtel Saint-Pol, as the rue Neuve-Saint-Paul. It was renamed rue Charles-V in 1864 after the king who built the Hôtel Saint-Pol.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: A street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, laid out in the early 13th century, known as the rue d'Orléans(-Saint-Marcel). It was renamed after the naturalist Louis Daubenton.

places.note: rue du Grand-Chantier, now part of rue des Archives
places.summary: The rue du Grand-Chantier ran between the rue des Haudriettes and the rue Pastourelle. It became part of the rue des Archives, named after the National Archives in the nearby Hôtel de Soubise.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: In the early 14th century the rue de l'Échelle du Temple, in 1450 the rue des Deux-Portes, later the rue des Quatre-Fils-Aymon, after the heroes of a medieval romance — probably from a shop sign. The name has since been shortened to rue des Quatre-Fils.

places.summary: The rue de Paradis in the Marais, between the rue Vieille-du-Temple and the rue des Archives. It was joined to the rue des Francs-Bourgeois in 1868.

places.summary: Already mentioned in 13th-century deeds as the 'old rue du Temple'. Over the centuries it was also called rue de la Couture du Temple and rue Barbette, after the Porte Barbette in Philip Augustus's wall.

places.summary: The rue des Poulies, near the Marais. The rue des Francs-Bourgeois, named after almshouses whose residents were exempt from taxes, absorbed several neighbouring streets in 1868 and 1893.

places.note: probably a second label on the Vieille rue du Temple
places.summary: Probably a second label on the same street as the 'Vieille rue du Temple' nearby; the poet Guillot called it simply the rue du Temple in 1300.

places.summary: The rue des Singes in the Marais, probably named after a shop sign. It was made part of the rue des Guillemites in 1868.

places.summary: Already built up and bearing this name in 1230. It is the heart of the Pletzl, the historic Jewish quarter of the Marais.

places.summary: Recorded as the rue de l'Écofle in 1233; an escoufle is a kite (the bird of prey), probably from a shop sign. The name evolved through Escoufle and Escoufles into Écouffes.

places.summary: Recorded under many spellings — rue Payelle, Parelle, des Payens, de Guienne. On this map it is the rue des Paiens.

places.summary: Named after Charles of Anjou, king of Sicily and brother of Saint Louis, who had a house here. In 1868 it absorbed the rue de Bercy-Saint-Jean, which this map labels separately as the rue Bouquetonne.

places.summary: A short street in the Marais, the rue des Ballets or Ballays. It is now part of the rue Malher.

places.summary: Built up by 1250 as the rue Renaut-le-Fèvre. In the 17th century it was called the rue Cloche-Percée — from a sign showing a pierced bell — and the name later became Cloche-Perce.

places.summary: The street of the abbot of Jouy, who had his Paris house here in the 13th century; part of it was later called the rue de la Fausse-Poterne-Saint-Paul. The reading 'Petit Ioui' on the label is uncertain.

places.summary: In existence in 1300, under names such as rue Frogier-l'Asnier and rue Forgier-l'Asnier, after a man who lived here; the name later became Geoffroy-l'Asnier.

places.note: label reads Garnier sur l'Eau (old spelling: Garnier sur l'Yaue)
places.summary: A street near Saint-Gervais that ran down to the river: in 1257 the rue André-sur-l'Eau, then Garnier-sur-l'Yaue, the form on this map. Part of its old line became the allée des Justes-de-France in 2000.

places.summary: In existence in 1182, named after the nuns of the abbey of Hyères (Yerres) who had their Paris house here; the label reads 'Nonnaindières'.

places.summary: The rue Copeau, named after the mound of Coupeau (Copeau) where the Jardin des Plantes was later created. It was renamed in 1853 after the naturalist Lacépède.

places.note: the main street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, from the Porte Bordelles
places.summary: The 'great street of Saint-Marcel', on the line of the Roman road from Lutetia south towards Italy. It was the main street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, leading out from the Porte Bordelles; it is today's rue Mouffetard and its continuation.

places.summary: The rue de la Croix, between the old rue Phélipeaux and the rue du Vertbois. It was joined with neighbouring streets in 1851 to form the rue Volta, named after the Italian physicist.

places.note: printed R. DES FONTI and SEN upside-down
places.summary: In existence in the early 15th century, named after the fountains supplied by the springs of Belleville; earlier simply the rue des Fontaines.

places.note: rue Frépaux = rue Phélipeaux; later rue Phélipeaux
places.summary: The rue Frépaux (also Fripaux), later the rue Phélipeaux, near the Temple. It was destroyed when the rue Réaumur was cut through at the end of the 19th century.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: In 1282 the rue Richard-des-Poulies, later the rue Portefoin. In the 17th century it was also called the rue des Enfants-Rouges, after the orphanage nearby.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: Recorded as the rue Jehan-de-Saint-Quentin in 1302 and as the rue Pastourelle around 1330, perhaps after a Roger Pastourel who owned land here.

places.summary: In existence in 1292, then called the rue Robert-Bégon or Capon, later the rue du Coq; its eastern part was the rue du Cimetière-Saint-Nicolas until 1851.

places.summary: The main road north from the Hôtel de Ville to the Temple enclosure. Its southern stretches had other names — rue des Coquilles, rue Barre-du-Bec, rue Sainte-Avoie — until they were all joined as the rue du Temple.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: The eastern part of today's rue de Montmorency: in 1328 the 'ruelle au Villain', later the rue Cour-au-Villain or Courtauvillain. It was joined to the rue de Montmorency in the 19th century.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: An old street of the Temple quarter, named after a Michel le Comte. During the Revolution (1793–1806) it was renamed after the deputy Michel Lepeletier.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: Named after the Haudriettes, a community of widows founded by Étienne Haudry. In 1290 it was the rue Jehan-l'Huilier; it has also been called rue de l'Échelle-du-Temple.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: A street opened by the Templars, first called the rue des Boucheries-du-Temple; it later took the name of the chapel of Braque, which stood on it.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: Named after the 'white mantles', mendicant friars (Servites) who settled here in 1258. In the 13th century it was the rue de la Parcheminerie.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: The rue du Puits in the Marais, named after a well. It was renamed in 1867 after Hugues Aubriot, provost of Paris under Charles V.

places.note: rue de l'Homme-Armé, now part of rue des Archives
places.summary: The rue de l'Homme-Armé ('street of the armed man', after a shop sign). It is now part of the rue des Archives.

places.summary: In 1232 the rue de Lagny, called 'de la Grande Bretonnerie'. Its name comes from the priory of Sainte-Croix-de-la-Bretonnerie that stood on it.

places.summary: In the late 13th century the rue du Franc-Mourier (or Franc-Meurier); by 1644 it was already called the rue de Moussy.

places.summary: In existence in the 13th century; in the 16th century it was the rue Chartron, 'called des Mauvais-Garçons' (of the bad boys), after the mercenaries who stayed here in the 1520s.

places.summary: The weavers' street (tisserands), recorded as Tixeranderie in 1263. It ran from the rue Jean-Pain-Mollet to the place Baudoyer and was destroyed when the rue de Rivoli was cut through in the 1850s.

places.summary: A street behind Saint-Jean-en-Grève with the earthy name of rue du Pet-au-Diable ('devil's fart'), after a boundary stone. Later called the rue du Tourniquet-Saint-Jean, it disappeared when the Hôtel de Ville was enlarged.

places.summary: Named after the mill of the Barres; in 1250 the 'ruelle au Moulin des Barres', later the rue du Chevet-Saint-Gervais, as it runs behind the apse of Saint-Gervais.

places.summary: Recorded in 1212; first the rue de la Foulerie (fullers), then the rue de la Mortellerie (mortar-makers). It runs behind the Hôtel de Ville and was renamed accordingly; part of it was demolished in the 1850s.

places.summary: An old street of the Saint-Martin quarter, named after the mayor (maire) of the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. The label spells it 'Au Mere'.

places.summary: A short street between the rue Saint-Victor and the rue Traversine, recorded as 'Pavée' in 1243 and later called rue du Mûrier and rue Pavée-d'Andouilles. It was destroyed when the rue des Écoles was cut through.

places.summary: The rue du Cimetière-Saint-Nicolas, along the cemetery of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs, opened around 1220. In 1851 it was made part of the rue Chapon.

places.summary: The rue des Petits-Champs in the Saint-Martin quarter, renamed rue Brantôme in 1864. It disappeared in the clearance of the Beaubourg plateau; a modern rue Brantôme near the Centre Pompidou revives the name.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: Recorded as the rue Marivas in 1280, later the rue Marivaux. It was renamed in 1851 after Nicolas Flamel, the scribe and bookseller who lived here and whom legend made an alchemist.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: A small street near Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie, named after a man called Jean Pain-Mollet ('soft bread'). It was destroyed when the rue de Rivoli was cut through.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: The cutlers' street, created at the end of the 12th century and widened in 1564. Earlier names include rue de la Vieille-Oreille and rue Guillori.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: The tanners' street, running from the place de Grève to the rue Saint-Martin, earlier the rue de l'Écorcherie (flaying). It was destroyed when the avenue Victoria was built.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: A street on the north side of the Cité, called Glateingni by Guillot in 1300 and also the rue du Val-d'Amour, as it was a street of brothels. It was destroyed in 1865 to build the new Hôtel-Dieu.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: Built in 1163, when Notre-Dame was begun, to bring building materials to the cathedral; it ran from the parvis to the rue du Marché-Palu. It was absorbed into the enlarged parvis in the 19th century.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: In existence in the early 13th century; in 1247 the street of the plasterers (rue des Plâtriers), later the rue du Plâtre. It was renamed after the jurist Jean Domat.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.note: rue des Noyers, absorbed by boulevard Saint-Germain
places.summary: The rue des Noyers (walnut trees) on the Left Bank. It was absorbed by the boulevard Saint-Germain in the 1850s.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: Opened as the rue du Clos-Bruneau and later called rue Saint-Hilaire (1322); it takes its present name from the Carmelite convent on the place Maubert.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: Opened in the early 14th century on the Clos Bruneau, a vineyard. It takes its name from the college of Dormans-Beauvais, whose chapel still stands on it.

places.note: printed LE CLOS BRVNIAV; rue du Clos-Bruneau
places.summary: The rue du Clos-Bruneau, named after a vineyard on the slope of the montagne Sainte-Geneviève; in 1243 the rue Judas. It was mostly destroyed by the boulevard Saint-Germain.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: The ancient Roman road south from the Seine, the cardo of Lutetia, and the start of the pilgrimage road to Santiago de Compostela. In the Middle Ages its stretches had many names, such as the grand'rue du Petit-Pont.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: The rue du Battoir(-Saint-André), the 'Haulte Rue dite du Bastouer'. In 1851 it was joined to the rue Serpente.

sources.label: Ville de Paris, street register (open data)

places.summary: A village east of Paris, here called 'Montreuil-sur-le-Bois', near the forest of Vincennes. It is now Montreuil, a large town in Seine-Saint-Denis.
A village on the Seine east of Paris, with riverside estates and, later, wine warehouses. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now part of the 12th arrondissement.
A village at the confluence of the Seine and the Marne, with a country house of the archbishops of Paris. It is now part of Charenton-le-Pont.
A village on the Seine south-east of Paris, now Ivry-sur-Seine.
A village on the Seine south-east of Paris, now Vitry-sur-Seine.
A village on the road south from Paris, now Villejuif.
A village on the Bièvre south of Paris, now Gentilly. Part of its territory was annexed to Paris in 1860.
The ruined castle of Bicêtre, south of Paris. Louis XIII had a hospital for invalid soldiers built on the site; it later became the Hôpital Bicêtre, in Le Kremlin-Bicêtre.
A village on a hill north-east of Paris, whose springs supplied the city's fountains. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 (19th and 20th arrondissements).
A village east of Paris, now Bagnolet.
A village east of Paris, on the site of a Merovingian royal residence. It was absorbed into the faubourg Saint-Antoine and is now a quarter of the 12th arrondissement.

places.note: the hamlet of Popincourt outside the wall; its name survives in the rue Popincourt
places.summary: A hamlet north-east of the city, outside the wall. Its name survives in the rue Popincourt and the Popincourt quarter of the 11th arrondissement.
A hamlet on the road to Belleville, known for its taverns: just outside the city, wine escaped the city's toll. It is now the area around the rue du Faubourg-du-Temple and Belleville.

places.note: the marais: market gardens on the old marshland north of the wall (today the 10th arrondissement), not the Marais district
places.summary: The marais, market gardens on the old marshland north of the city wall, where vegetables for Paris were grown. Today the area is part of the 10th arrondissement; the Marais district inside the walls has the same origin.
The suburb along the road north from the Porte Saint-Martin, around the church of Saint-Laurent and the Saint-Laurent fair.
The suburb along the road north from the Porte Saint-Denis towards the abbey of Saint-Denis. The rue du Faubourg-Saint-Denis follows its main street.

A suburb north of the city walls, the Villeneuve-sur-Gravois, where the church of Notre-Dame-de-Bonne-Nouvelle was built in the 16th century. It was destroyed during the siege of 1591 and later rebuilt; it is the Bonne-Nouvelle quarter of today.
A hamlet on the north side of the hill of Montmartre, now the Clignancourt quarter of the 18th arrondissement.
The hill north of Paris with its village and the Benedictine abbey of Montmartre. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now the 18th arrondissement.
A fortified farm north-west of the city, belonging to the bishops of Paris and later the Hôtel-Dieu, on a stream of the same name. The rue de la Grange-Batelière (9th arrondissement) keeps its name.

The suburb that grew up around the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés outside Philip Augustus's wall, with the Saint-Germain fair. In the 17th and 18th centuries it became the most aristocratic quarter of Paris.
A hamlet north-west of the city with a manor house, later known for its open-air taverns. It is now part of the 9th arrondissement.
The suburb along the road west from the Porte Saint-Honoré. The rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré follows its main street; the Élysée palace stands on it.
A village west of the city belonging to the bishop of Paris, hence its name (the bishop's town). The rue de la Ville-l'Évêque, near the Madeleine, keeps its name.
A village on the road west from Paris, with a leper house. It was absorbed into the faubourg Saint-Honoré; the church of Saint-Philippe-du-Roule keeps its name.
A village on the hill west of Paris above the Seine. It was annexed in 1860; the Palais de Chaillot stands at the top of the hill.
A village west of Paris on the Seine, later a favourite country retreat of writers such as Molière and Boileau. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now part of the 16th arrondissement.
